payload.explanation_text:
A cell membrane surrounds a cell and controls what moves in and out, so it regulates exchange with the cell's surroundings.

Phospholipids are the building blocks of this membrane. Each phospholipid is amphipathic, which means it has two different parts. Its head is hydrophilic (water-loving), and its fatty acid tails are hydrophobic (water-avoiding). Because of this, phospholipids in water arrange themselves into a bilayer: the heads face the water on both sides, and the tails are tucked inside. Each of the two layers is called a leaflet.

Fatty acids are carbon chains. A saturated chain has no carbon–carbon double bonds, so its tail can pack closely with its neighbors. A tail with double bonds is unsaturated. Those double bonds create bends in the tail, which hinder close packing and increase fluidity. Fluidity means how freely the membrane's components can move.

Several factors affect fluidity: saturation, chain length, temperature, and cholesterol.

Cholesterol acts as a buffer for fluidity. It restrains excessive movement, and it helps prevent the membrane from becoming stiff when it is cold.

The fluid mosaic model describes the membrane as a mixture of lipids, cholesterol, and proteins. These components can move sideways within the membrane.

The two leaflets are not identical; they differ in composition. Lipids seldom move from one leaflet to the other on their own. Flippases, floppases, and scramblases help this movement.

Carbohydrate chains on the outer surface of the membrane form the glycocalyx, also called the sugar coating. The glycocalyx supports cell recognition and helps the cell distinguish self from non-self.

concepts.name: Amphipathic phospholipids form the bilayer
concepts.taught_summary: Phospholipids have a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic fatty acid tails. In water they form a bilayer with heads facing water on both sides and tails inside, and each layer is a leaflet.

concepts.name: Saturated vs. unsaturated fatty acids
concepts.taught_summary: Saturated fatty acid chains lack carbon–carbon double bonds and pack closely. Double bonds in unsaturated tails create bends that hinder packing and increase fluidity.

concepts.name: What affects membrane fluidity
concepts.taught_summary: Fluidity means how freely membrane components move. Saturation, chain length, temperature, and cholesterol affect fluidity.

concepts.name: Cholesterol as a fluidity buffer
concepts.taught_summary: Cholesterol buffers fluidity: it restrains excessive movement and helps prevent cold-induced stiffening.

concepts.name: Fluid mosaic model
concepts.taught_summary: The fluid mosaic model describes a mixture of lipids, cholesterol, and proteins, with components moving sideways.

concepts.name: Membrane asymmetry and lipid flipping
concepts.taught_summary: The two leaflets differ in composition. Lipids seldom switch leaflets unaided; flippases, floppases, and scramblases assist this movement.

concepts.name: Glycocalyx and cell recognition
concepts.taught_summary: Outer-surface carbohydrate chains form the glycocalyx, or sugar coating, which supports cell recognition and self/non-self distinction.
